title: Hooke's Law with a Spring
subtitle: Stretch a spring, watch the restoring force grow, and find how stiffness and mass set the oscillation.
objectives: Calculate the spring force from the stretch and spring constant using F = kx.
Predict how the restoring-force arrow changes when the stretch is doubled.
Explain how the spring constant affects the force and the oscillation period.

formulas.meaning: Hooke's law: the spring force grows in proportion to the stretch.
Elastic energy stored in a stretched spring.
Period of one full oscillation; it does not depend on the stretch.

debrief: The spring force is proportional to the stretch: double the stretch and you double the force. A stiffer spring (larger k) gives more force and a shorter period, while a heavier block swings more slowly.

levels.title: Force from stretch
levels.goal: The spring constant is 20 N/m. Set the stretch so the spring pulls with a force of 10 N.
hints: Hooke's law says $F = k\,x$, so the force is 20 times the stretch.
You need $20 \times x = 10$; divide 10 by 20 to find the stretch in metres.

feedback.say: That is still the starting stretch of 0.2 m.
The spring force is now {Fmag} N.

levels.solutionText: $F = k\,x = 20 \times 0.5 = 10\,\text{N}$, so the stretch must be $x = \dfrac{10}{20} = 0.5\,\text{m}$.
levels.explain: With a fixed spring constant the force is proportional to the stretch: 10 N needs a stretch of 0.5 m at 20 N/m.

levels.title: Double the stretch
levels.goal: The spring (30 N/m) is stretched 0.1 m and pulls with 3 N. Double the stretch and watch what happens to the force.
hints: Doubling 0.1 m gives 0.2 m of stretch.
Hooke's law is proportional: if $x$ doubles, $F = k\,x$ doubles too.

feedback.say: The stretch has not changed yet.
You quadrupled the stretch; doubling 0.1 m gives 0.2 m.
The spring force is now {Fmag} N.

levels.solutionText: Double the stretch: $x = 0.2\,\text{m}$. Then $F = 30 \times 0.2 = 6\,\text{N}$, exactly twice 3 N.
levels.explain: Hooke's law is linear: doubling the stretch doubles the restoring force, whatever the spring constant is.

levels.title: A stiffer spring
levels.goal: Keep the stretch at 0.2 m. Choose a spring constant so the force becomes 16 N.
hints: The stretch stays at 0.2 m, so only $k$ changes.

feedback.say: Doubling k to 40 N/m gives 8 N; you need twice that.
The spring force is now {Fmag} N.

levels.explain: At the same stretch, the force is proportional to the spring constant: a stiffer spring pulls four times as hard if k is four times as large.

levels.title: Predict the energy
levels.goal: A spring with k = 50 N/m is stretched 0.2 m. How much elastic energy is stored in it? Type your prediction before checking.

feedback.say: Close, but you forgot the factor of one half in the formula.
You forgot to square the stretch: 0.2 squared is 0.04, not 0.2.

levels.explain: Energy grows with the square of the stretch, so it is not proportional the way force is: doubling the stretch would quadruple the energy.

levels.title: Tune the period
levels.goal: Keep the stretch at 0.2 m and choose the spring constant and block mass so one full oscillation takes about 1.26 s. Press Release to watch it swing.
hints: The period does not depend on the stretch at all, so leave it alone.

feedback.say: Too fast: soften the spring or add mass to slow it down. The period is {T} s.
Too slow: stiffen the spring or lighten the block. The period is {T} s.

levels.explain: The period depends only on the mass and the spring constant: more mass or a softer spring means a slower oscillation, and the stretch plays no role.
